sources.note: Read held by the project: the thesis describes Sare (Kapriman, kapr1245) only; p.2 'Of the Sepik Hill Family, to which Sare belongs, only Alamblak (Bruce 1984), has a comprehensive description'; the explicit stress rule (2.2.1, pp.40-42: secondary stress initial, primary stress final in disyllables and penultimate in longer words) is for Sare alone; nothing on this language.

Appendix 9.2 wordlist (pp.260-264) has a Piame column whose phonetic forms carry stress ticks on a minority of items (p.262: məfu'aiwo 'lies down', məmini'nɔni 'man', ka'lami 'neck', pasiti'ɔwa 'moon', ye'lia 'meat', bəubiy'eipa 'old man') with no explanation of the notation and no prose on stress; 0 hits for stress/accent/tone in the text.

X is footnote 1 on thesis p. 513 (section X.E.2.c 'Morphological change'), about OTHER Sepik Hill languages: 'Lewis and Lewis (1970) indicate that stress occurs on the first syllable of the word in Sanio-Hiowe. sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. & John Z'graggen. 1975. The Sepik-Ramu Phylum. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 731-763. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/252975.
sources.note: 0 occurrences of stress/accent/pitch in the chapter; 'tonal' occurs only re Abau/Iwam/Wogamusin (Upper Sepik: the Baileys 'claim to have established tonal contrasts in the verb morphology', contra Laycock 1965b). General 'Sepik-Ramu phonology' remarks (few vowels, plain vs prenasalised stops) only; nothing on Sepik Hill prosody and nothing on Piame beyond the population figure.

Of the three new groups contacted by the patrol the BIAMI appear to have the only completely new language'.
